brief.greeting: Good morning. The kernel shipped another prepatch while AI researchers tried to lattice‑ify the universe.

stories.headline: Linux 7.4‑rc3 lands with driver tweaks
stories.body: **Small updates, big impact:** The 7.4‑rc3 prepatch is out, mostly polishing drivers. It’s a test release, so expect a few regressions before final.
stories.why: If you write or maintain drivers, this is the code you’ll be compiling next week.

stories.headline: GPT‑6 helps define Standard Model on lattice
stories.body: **AI meets particle physics:** Researchers used GPT‑6 Astra to draft a non‑perturbative lattice definition of the Standard Model, producing a detailed proof that was previously out of reach.
stories.why: Shows how large language models can accelerate theoretical work you might cite in a paper.

stories.headline: SunshineStream offers self‑hosted game streaming
stories.body: **C++ server for Moonlight clients:** SunshineStream’s new repo lets you run a lightweight streaming server on any PC, compatible with the popular Moonlight client.
stories.why: Great for engineers who want low‑latency remote gaming without a cloud subscription.

highlights.title: Kernel prepatch 7.4-rc3
highlights.summary: Linux kernel 7.4‑rc3 prepatch was released for testing, with most changes being small driver updates.
highlights.detail: Linus Torvalds described the release as “fairly normal,” noting networking and GPU drivers contributed the bulk of modifications. The patch set continues the usual release‑candidate cadence ahead of the final 7.4 launch.

related.title: Three new stable kernels for Tuesday

highlights.title: A step toward defining the Standard Model on a lattice
highlights.summary: A candidate nonperturbative lattice definition of the Standard Model was explored, with GPT‑6 Astra assisting in producing a detailed proof.
highlights.detail: The work proposes a concrete formulation of the Standard Model on a discrete spacetime lattice, aiming to bypass perturbative limitations. GPT‑6 Astra was used to automate parts of the derivation, demonstrating AI's role in theoretical physics. The approach remains speculative and requires further validation against known particle physics results.

highlights.title: LVMH’s Media Division announces strategic partnership with OpenAI
highlights.summary: LVMH’s Media Division and OpenAI announced a partnership to integrate AI tools into journalism and improve accessibility via ChatGPT.
highlights.detail: The collaboration will provide LVMH’s publications with AI‑generated summaries, translations, and interactive features. It aims to streamline content creation and reach broader audiences, while both parties emphasize responsible AI use. No financial terms were disclosed.

highlights.title: Our new blog for science
highlights.summary: OpenAI launched a science‑focused blog to share research findings, practical AI methods, and user experiences in scientific discovery.
highlights.detail: The blog will feature posts from internal and external researchers, covering topics from model‑driven experiments to AI‑assisted data analysis. It serves as a centralized venue for the community to track how AI is applied across scientific domains.

highlights.title: SunshineStream/Sunshine
highlights.summary: SunshineStream is a C++ self‑hosted game‑streaming server compatible with Moonlight clients.
highlights.detail: The repository includes source code for encoding video frames and handling input latency. It targets low‑power PCs and can be compiled on Linux, offering an open‑source alternative to proprietary streaming solutions.

items.title: An Orbital Sanders Crash Course and the Threat of HAVS
items.summary: A Hackaday article explains how orbital sanders work and highlights the occupational hazard of hand‑arm vibration syndrome (HAVS).
items.detail: The piece details the mechanics of orbital sanding tools and presents safety guidelines to mitigate vibration exposure. It cites medical studies linking prolonged use to nerve damage, urging users to adopt protective equipment and limit session length.

items.title: Follow The Grid With An Arduino Uno
items.summary: A tutorial shows how to use an Arduino Uno to detect the 50 Hz or 60 Hz mains frequency by sampling the AC grid waveform.
items.detail: The guide explains wiring the Arduino to a voltage divider and using interrupt timing to measure zero‑crossings. It discusses handling both US and European standards and provides sample code for real‑time frequency display.

items.title: Hackaday Links: November 15, 2026
items.summary: Hackaday Supercon recap published on November 15, 2026 notes record attendance and a new venue with excess capacity.
items.detail: The event featured expanded speaker line‑ups and additional workshops compared to prior years. Organizers highlighted improved networking spaces and a larger exhibition hall, suggesting the conference is scaling sustainably.

items.title: It’s A NAS, For Sony Mavica Disks
items.summary: An article examines a discontinued Sony Mavica‑compatible NAS that stored images on proprietary disks.
items.detail: The piece places the device in the early digital camera era, noting its limited market lifespan of only a few years before SD cards became dominant. It also details the hardware’s reliance on legacy ATA interfaces.

items.title: Loop Antennas for Transmitting
items.summary: A guide compares loop antennas to traditional outdoor designs, highlighting their compact size and trade‑offs for amateur radio operators.
items.detail: Loop antennas offer lower visual impact and easier indoor installation but typically have reduced gain and bandwidth. The article provides construction tips and performance measurements for common loop dimensions.

items.title: SunshineStream/Sunshine
items.summary: SunshineStream is a C++ self‑hosted game‑streaming server compatible with Moonlight clients.
items.detail: The repository includes source code for encoding video frames and handling input latency. It targets low‑power PCs and can be compiled on Linux, offering an open‑source alternative to proprietary streaming solutions.

items.title: google-labs-code/stitch-skills
items.summary: stitch-skills provides a library of Agent Skills for the Stitch MCP server, adhering to the Agent Skills open standard.
items.detail: Skills are pre‑built modules that enable coding agents like Antigravity, Gemini CLI, Claude Code, and Cursor to perform tasks such as file manipulation and API calls. The library is written in Python and designed for easy extension.

items.title: ManimCommunity/manim
items.summary: ManimCommunity/manim is a community-maintained Python library for generating mathematical animations.
items.detail: The project continues the original Manim framework, adding community contributions and updated documentation. It supports vector graphics, LaTeX rendering, and integrates with Jupyter notebooks. The library is open source under the MIT license and is frequently updated on GitHub.

items.title: huytieu/COG-second-brain
items.summary: COG-second-brain is a self‑evolving personal knowledge system offering 35 AI skills, 10 autonomous agents, and a built‑in CRM.
items.detail: It uses a V‑model verification lifecycle to prevent agents from grading their own output, improving reliability. The system integrates with Claude Code, Cursor, Kiro, Gemini CLI, and Codex, enabling code generation and UI design assistance. Designed for marketing and product teams, it includes anti‑slop design patterns.

items.title: Canner/WrenAI
items.summary: WrenAI provides GenBI, an open‑source text‑to‑SQL layer that creates trusted dashboards from natural‑language queries across 20+ data sources.
items.detail: Supported backends include BigQuery, Snowflake, PostgreSQL, ClickHouse, Amazon Redshift, and Databricks. The system adds governance by exposing the generated SQL for review, reducing hallucination risk. It aims to simplify business intelligence for developers and data analysts without proprietary SaaS.

items.title: PrefectHQ/fastmcp
items.summary: fastmcp is a Pythonic library for quickly building MCP (Message Control Protocol) servers and clients.
items.detail: The package offers high‑performance asynchronous I/O and a concise API for defining message schemas. It includes utilities for connection management, serialization, and testing. The project targets developers needing lightweight, scalable inter‑process communication in Python.
